title: No Representation Until Two Hours Ago: the Chancellor's Own Timeline, 11 May 1866
participants: The Chancellor of the Exchequer (not named in the record)
Bank of England, Governor and Deputy Governor

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: No skim is documented here, and this dossier does not invent one. What the record shows at the front end is a discount house failure announced the previous day and a Bank of England that had, that same day, "extended its loans and discounts to-day to a sum of something more than £4,000,000" — private credit expanded against a reserve that could not carry it.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The structural fact is in the Bank's own balance sheet as the Chancellor reported it to the House: "we find the Bank reserves reduced in a single day from a sum approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000." Half the reserve of the country's central bank went in one day, under a statute — the Bank Charter Act 1844 — that fixed a limit the Bank was now about to exceed.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is visible in the question rather than the answer. Mr Disraeli rose to ask "Whether there is any truth in the prevalent rumour that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any relaxation of the provisions of the Bank Charter regulating the issue of notes?" — a rumour was circulating in the City about a government decision the Chancellor then stated had not been taken. Meanwhile the Chancellor told the House he was "not yet cognizant of the actual state of affairs in the City, as it is exhibited from time to time by the accounts of the Bank of England": the minister deciding was behind the market he was deciding about.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was an indemnity, granted the same evening and addressed to one institution. The Government determined "to address a letter to the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank" recommending that if the Bank found occasion "to make such advances from the Issue Department as shall exceed the limits allowed by law", it "should not hesitate to make that issue", with the Government undertaking "to make immediate application to Parliament to sanction that proceeding". The statutory limit was set aside by letter, with retrospective parliamentary cover promised.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There is no inquiry in this record to whitewash anything — the containment is in the diagnosis offered to the House on the night. The uneasiness, the Chancellor said, "does not arise from any general unsoundness in the condition of our commercial relations, but only from causes of a peculiar and specific character." A systemic event was characterised, within hours and before any investigation, as a local and specific one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Bank Charter Act 1844, and two existing precedents for suspending it — the letters of 1847 and 1857, which the Chancellor cited by date as the model for what he was about to do.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A third letter on the same terms, which is what turns two exceptions into a standing practice. The Chancellor's own words make the inheritance explicit: the letter was to be "substantially the same as was addressed to those high officers in 1847 and 1857".
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The Bank lends to sustain commerce; lending drains the reserve; the drained reserve is the reason the statutory limit must be lifted; lifting the limit lets the lending continue. Each turn of the loop is also the precedent for the next, which is why there was a form of words ready in 1866.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Government and the Bank of England had the rescue prepared in advance — that insiders knew the crash was coming, positioned for it, and the suspension of the Bank Charter Act was the payoff arranged beforehand.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: It fails on the best available evidence against it, which is the Chancellor's own account given under hostile questioning from Disraeli in the same sitting. He said there was "no truth in the statement that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any step to be taken at variance with the provisions of the Act of 1844"; that "they have not arrived at any decision"; that "until two hours or two hours and a half ago no representation or formal report of any kind had reached me from the City"; and — the detail hardest to reconcile with a prepared plan — "I have not the least reason to suppose that any request from that quarter", the Directors of the Bank of England, "is likely to reach the Government." Later the same evening he described "the extraordinary rapidity with which the crisis has come upon us, and which has reduced the opportunity of deliberation given to the Government within very narrow limits indeed." A minister can lie to the House, and this dossier cannot exclude it. But the version the record supports is worse than the conspiracy in a specific way: there was no plan, there was a form of words from 1847 and 1857, and an afternoon was enough. What the record DOES show is who moved it. Not the Bank — the banks: "gentlemen representing in particular the private banks of London" came first, then "a deputation regularly constituted from the joint-stock banks in London", and their representations "were pressed even more earnestly and urgently than I anticipated". The requisition came from the creditors, and the statute was set aside between their arrival and the close of business.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Two exchanges in the House of Commons on 11 May 1866, printed in Hansard at vol 183 cc772-4 and cc840-2. In the first, the Chancellor of the Exchequer states that no decision has been taken, that no representation had reached him until two to two and a half hours earlier, that he has since received an "important requisition" and seen "many of the most influential and respected members of the body of the London bankers" with a joint-stock bank deputation expected, that those bankers describe the panic as "without parallel in the recollection of the oldest men of business in the City of London" and "suggest and desire that in some form or other relief should be afforded", and that he has no reason to expect any request from the Bank of England's directors. In the second, hours later, he reports that the Bank has lent more than £4,000,000 that day, that its reserves fell in a single day from approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000, and that the Government has determined to send the Governor and Deputy Governor a letter substantially the same as those of 1847 and 1857, authorising issue beyond the legal limit with a promise of retrospective parliamentary sanction. He attributes the crisis not to "any general unsoundness" but to "causes of a peculiar and specific character", and notes the extraordinary rapidity with which it arrived. NEITHER DOCUMENT NAMES THE FAILED FIRM: the Chancellor refers only to "the calamitous event announced yesterday", and the word "Overend" appears nowhere in either page. The letter itself, the Bank's records, and any account of who gained or lost were not read.

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE PANIC IN THE CITY" — QUESTION, HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc772-4 (Historic Hansard, 1803–2005)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. (The URL slug is "question-5" because the service names child items of a debate heading by position; it is reached from the sitting index for 11 May 1866 and the page header reads "THE PANIC IN THE CITY. / QUESTION. / HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc772-4".) THE FIRM IS NOT NAMED. Nowhere in this exchange, or in the Bank Charter Act exchange later the same evening, does the word "Overend" appear; the Chancellor refers only to "the calamitous event announced yesterday". This dossier therefore takes the identification of the failed house from its own title and not from this document. WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS. MR. DISRAELI opened: "I take this opportunity of inquiring of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Whether there is any truth in the prevalent rumour that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any relaxation of the provisions of the Bank Charter regulating the issue of notes?" MR. BAZLEY and MR. BIDDULPH pressed the same point, Mr Biddulph asking "whether he is prepared to relax the provisions of the Bank Act in the event of the Bank directors making a proposition to that effect". THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER replied — and his answer is a timeline given under questioning: "there is no truth in the statement that Her Majesty's Government have authorized any step to be taken at variance with the provisions of the Act of 1844. In point of fact, they have not arrived at any decision upon the subject of the state of things which prevails in the City in immediate connection with the calamitous event announced yesterday. I may go further and say, that until two hours or two hours and a half ago no representation or formal report of any kind had reached me from the City upon the subject of the existing state of things; but for the last two hours and a half my time has been occupied in receiving information and statements, and, I may add, an important requisition from very influential persons connected with the City." ON WHO CAME: "I have seen many of the most influential and respected members of the body of the London bankers on the subject, and I have not yet had time to see, but I expect to see as soon as my engagements in this House will allow me to leave my place, a deputation regularly constituted from the joint-stock banks in London to the same effect." ON WHAT THEY SAID: "The purport of the statements made by them is that they conceive the state of panic and distress which prevails in the City to be without parallel in the recollection of the oldest men of business in the City of London. They suggest and desire that in some form or other relief should be afforded." ON THE BANK OF ENGLAND, which had not asked: "The hon. Gentleman behind me has asked me whether we should consent to suspend the Bank Act in the event of the Directors of the Bank of England making a proposition to that effect. On that question I should wish to make this remark: in the first place, having stated our anxiety to proceed promptly with this matter, I think I had better not answer any question; especially any question relating to the hypothesis of a request by the Directors of the Bank of England, for I have not the least reason to suppose that any request from that quarter is likely to reach the Government." He also described the Bank as "the mirror of the monetary" state "of the country". THE SPEAKER IS NOT NAMED IN THE RECORD: Hansard identifies him only as "THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER", and this dossier does not name the individual, because this page does not. TRANSCRIPTION FAULTS IN THE DIGITISED TEXT, recorded so that nothing is quoted from them: the passage about the Bank reads "the mirror of the monetary slate of the country" and "from the the actual trans actions of the Bank" — "slate" for "state" and a split word, which are artefacts of the digitisation, not of the 1866 text. Quotations above avoid those phrases or mark the substitution.

citations.title: House of Commons, "SUSPENSION OF THE BANK CHARTER ACT." — QUESTION, HC Deb 11 May 1866 vol 183 cc840-2 (Historic Hansard, 1803–2005)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service. This is the SAME SITTING as the "Panic in the City" exchange, some hours later — the two are the morning and the evening of 11 May 1866, and read together they are a decision being taken inside a single afternoon. MR. BAZLEY asked "Whether he has consented to recommend any peculiar facilities to be extended to the Bank of England during the existing monetary panic". THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER answered: "I stated, in the commencement of the evening, that representations had been made to me from quarters of the greatest influence and credit with respect to the extraordinary state of alarm and distress prevailing in the City to-day. I stated that those representations had come to me from gentlemen representing in particular the private banks of London, and I expected that I should shortly receive similar representations from those connected with the joint-stock banks. Those representations I have received accordingly, and they were pressed even more earnestly and urgently than I anticipated." THE NUMBERS THE GOVERNMENT ACTED ON: "we find that the Bank, moved by a just desire to sustain the commerce of the country, and to avert disaster, has extended its loans and discounts to-day to a sum of something more than £4,000,000. The effect of that large accommodation was to reduce the reserves of the Bank to a sum not very far short of £3,000,000 of money" — and, stated again, "we find the Bank reserves reduced in a single day from a sum approaching £6,000,000 to a little exceeding £3,000,000." THE DECISION, AND ITS PRECEDENT: "we have determined to address a letter to the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank, substantially the same as was addressed to those high officers in 1847 and 1857. That is to say, if the Bank, proceeding upon its usual prudent rules of administration, shall find occasion, in order to meet the wants of legitimate commerce, to make such advances from the Issue Department as shall exceed the limits allowed by law, we recommend that they should not hesitate to make that issue, and we undertake, in the event of the arrival of that contingency, to make immediate application to Parliament to sanction that proceeding." ON HOW LITTLE TIME THERE WAS — the sentence that bears directly on any claim of a prepared plan: "there is also another distinction, and that is the extraordinary rapidity with which the crisis has come upon us, and which has reduced the opportunity of deliberation given to the Government within very narrow limits indeed. We have not, however, hesitated to act". ON THE DIAGNOSIS OFFERED TO THE HOUSE: the uneasiness "does not arise from any general unsoundness in the condition of our commercial relations, but only from causes of a peculiar and specific character." WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT CONTAIN: the letter itself (promised "in the hands of the Governor and Deputy Governor of the Bank to-morrow") was not read; no Bank of England record was read; the failed house is never named; and there is nothing here about who profited, who was ruined, or what any private party knew in advance.
